text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- The ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party has agreed on a new working hours for hospital doctors.
- Austria to comply with the European Union's Schengen border agreement by October 27 next year, after plans to comply by July were scrapped because of mounting computer problems.
- Bank Austria may team up with Raiffeisen Zentralbank to bid for a 25 percent stake in postal saving's bank PSK, which is to be privatised.
- Papermaker Leykam looking for a strategic partner abroad, but Dutch KNP group insists it has no plans to sell the unit.
- Truck drivers' strike in France causes lack of supplies at Austrian car makers, threatening production.
- Austrian interest rates have reached the bottom, GiroCredit bank says.
DIE PRESSE
- Small family-owned shops should be allowed to remain open until 9 p.m. on weekdays, Economics Minister Hannes Farnleitner proposes.
- Federal tax revenue will rise by 66 billion schillings this year, deficit not to exceed planned 90 billion schillings, Finance Minister Viktor Klima says.
- Drug retail prices to fall up to five percent from February of next year.
- Grocery chain Billa says it will seek a court injunction against rival grocerer Spar's takeover of the familia retail chain of drugstores, citing cartel concerns.
- GiroCredit bank says it expects strong gains on Vienna's stock exchange next year.
- Baumax chief executive and majority owner Karlheinz Essl denies he intends to sell part of his group of do-it-yourself stores to German interests.
- Chief executive of Semperit, Austrian tyre making unit of Germany's Continental, has offered his resignation following Continental's plans to half production at the plant.
- Austrian banks' deadline for sporting goods maker HTM to pay back 190 million schillings in credits ends this week.
- Austria's state-owned printing company will be turned into a joint stock company next year to prepare it for privatisation.
KURIER
- Austrians will spend less money on christmas shopping this year because of rigid spending cuts and tax hikes by the Austrian government, analysts say.
- OPEC ministers meeting in Vienna decided to keep production quotas unchanged in order to avoid pressure on oil prices.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT

- The government may sell its stake in Bank Austria or in postal savings bank PSK should it not be able to realise revenues from the planned sale of Creditanstalt before year-end, Finance Minister Viktor Klima says.
